chapter_title: Chương 199: Bánh Màn Thầu – Án Mạng Kinh Hoàng

segments.title: Chương 199: Bánh Màn Thầu – Án Mạng Kinh Hoàng
segments.content:
Chapter 202, Part 0199: The Bloody Incident Triggered by a Steamed Bun. The growth of Weibo's paying users was faster than Chen Guiliang had anticipated.

He wanted to hype up the "Weibo" concept, but none of the major internet companies followed suit. Only a few media outlets mentioned it in passing.

*Internet Weekly* published an article to stir up readers' emotions, but it mainly focused on the Sino-Korean competition between Kaixin001 and Cyworld.

But it didn't matter!

As long as some media wrote a few lines about it, Bytedance could use it to create a narrative.

Xie Yang arranged for people to post on Tieba and forums every day, claiming that "Weibo" was the new direction for social networking and that all major Chinese internet companies were paying close attention.

Some netizens were inevitably drawn in.

The number of users activating mobile Weibo with payment was already increasing by more than 160 per day, a steady rise.

This was especially true for those with monthly phone bill subsidies. They had so much credit they couldn't use it all and had to go on a spending spree at the end of the month. As long as this group understood the concept of Weibo, they were more than willing to try something new; after all, it wasn't their own money they were spending.

These people would also spread mobile Weibo to their colleagues.

The conversations often went like this:

"Look, Yu Quan sent another multimedia message. Chen Yufan is walking his dog in the neighborhood."

"When was this?"

"Just now."

"How do you know?"

"Haha, I have his Weibo. I can get his updates anytime."

"That's so cool! How do you do that?"

"I'll show you how… Oh right, remember to 'super follow' me. A regular follow won't get you mobile Weibo updates."

It had truly become a fashion statement, something to show off.

The Zhongguancun Cinema was right next to Bytedance and Youke.

Although Chen Guiliang didn't care what they watched, he still offered a sincere reminder, "Actually, you might want to reconsider. Director Chen's films in recent years have been... hard to describe."

"I quite liked his *Farewell My Concubine*," Bian Guanyue said.

Chen Guiliang said, "*Farewell My Concubine* had everyone from the producer to the screenwriter, from the investors to the main actors, who could rein Director Chen in and keep him from getting carried away."

Chen Guiliang believed that *Farewell My Concubine* was indeed personally directed by Director Chen, because he genuinely had the skill. His father, on the other hand, couldn't have pulled it off.

It was just that this director was prone to letting himself go, and his train of thought was truly different from the average person's.

Bian Guanyue looked up at the movie schedule. Besides *The Promise*, there were also *Perhaps Love*, *Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire*, *The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe*, and *Her Majesty's Laughter*.

Not yet released, but scheduled for Christmas were: *A Chinese Tall Story*, *Riding Alone for thousands of Miles*, *King Kong*, and *The Shopaholics*.

"Let's go with *Perhaps Love* then." Bian Guanyue was mainly drawn to the words "musical film."

Chen Guiliang readily agreed, even though he had no feelings for the movie.

Chen Guiliang took Bian Guanyue to queue for tickets, and also bought some Coke and popcorn.

With 40 minutes until the movie started, the two found a corner to sit and chat.

"Listen to my song, *Nursery Rhyme*." Bian Guanyue handed him one of her MP3 earbuds.

Chen Guiliang took it with a smile. He had already heard it many times.

He had given Bian Guanyue the idea to write a Chinese-style song with opera-like vocals, but the result was completely different from what he'd imagined.

The main verse was a pop-style recitation in Sichuan dialect. The chorus was a high-pitched Sichuan opera vocal. The ending was like a nursery rhyme.

It sounded strange, yet it had a unique charm.

Chen Guiliang closed his eyes, and Bian Guanyue's imitation of a child's voice reciting in dialect came through the earbud:

"Bluestone slabs, hopscotch games, tiptoes shattering the morning dew.

Rolling iron hoops, clanging loud, chasing butterflies over the courtyard wall.

Grandma calls, come back inside, the smell of food tugs at my dress.

A sip of sweetness, a knock on malt candy, sticking to a child's old times."

In the middle, there was a main verse sung in a pop style.

Then came the faster-paced, high-pitched Sichuan opera vocals:

"A kite tugs its string, flying into the clouds.

A handful of mud, oh, molded into a small face.

Cicadas sing of long summer, the shade under the tree is a bed.

In dreams, the cattail fan sways and sways, shattering a river of bright starlight..."

The last part was a Sichuan nursery rhyme about hide-and-seek, the child's voice distant, gradually fading away.

To be honest, the transitions between the sections weren't very smooth. Bian Guanyue hadn't yet grasped the essence of the Chinese style. Her singing was too proper, not pop enough, not catchy enough.

It was a bit of a mishmash.

After listening to it with Chen Guiliang, Bian Guanyue said, "On my Xiaonei and Kaixin001 message boards, a lot of people said this song is well-written. But I still feel like something is off, there's a... um, a sense of disconnect."

Chen Guiliang suggested, "For the opening child's voice reciting in dialect, could you turn it into a dialect rap? It should be languid and casual, as if someone is lying in bed reminiscing about childhood. For the opera-style chorus, don't make it so traditional; try to make it more pop."

Bian Guanyue thought it over carefully. "I can try that."

She was truly bored most of the time. Besides classes, her only hobbies were writing songs and singing.

Just as Bian Guanyue was about to speak, Chen Guiliang raised an index finger to his lips and shushed her.

Chen Guiliang had spotted Guo Fengzi, queuing to buy movie tickets with a girl.

Just from Guo Feng's awkward demeanor, Chen Guiliang knew that the girl beside him was the legendary "Shijie."

Just as Senior Brother Min had said, this Shijie wasn't exceptionally beautiful.

But she gave off a very clean and pure feeling, as if untouched by the mundane world, like a secluded orchid blooming silently in a valley.

"Two half-price tickets for *The Promise*. We have student IDs."

A founding shareholder of the mighty Bytedance was pulling out a student ID to ask for a half-price ticket.

Guo Feng turned his head and asked, "Do you want a Coke?"

Shijie said, "Yes."

Guo Feng asked again, "Do you want popcorn?"

Shijie said, "Yes."

"Then I'll buy them for you." Guo Feng brightened up.

The two of them, holding Coke and popcorn, found a place to sit down.

Then, they didn't know what to talk about.

After building up his courage for a long time, Guo Feng finally asked, "Are you participating in a project?"

Shijie said, "Yeah, helping out my professor and senior classmates."

Guo Feng didn't know how to continue the conversation and blurted out, "This is my first time watching a movie in a theater."

Shijie said, "Me too."

"But I've seen them on the computer."

"I haven't. I watched VCDs in middle school. My dad likes martial arts movies."

"I heard *The Promise* is really good."

"I don't know."

"Have you seen *Farewell My Concubine*?"

"No."

"What about *A Chinese Odyssey*?"

"I heard my roommate mention it before."

Their conversation was like kindergarteners playing house.

In the screening hall.

Chen Guiliang was dozing off. He was trying very hard not to fall asleep.

Bian Guanyue, however, was watching with great interest. The musical film was right up her alley. But occasionally, she would furrow her brows, feeling that the plot wasn't to her liking.

After finally enduring *Perhaps Love*, Chen Guiliang stretched and left.

As they walked, Bian Guanyue said, "Jacky Cheung's character wasn't well-developed. He was like a tool just to move the plot forward. And the love in it... how should I put it? It seemed like they were loving for the sake of love. The motivation for their love lacked conviction. It was like the director assigned them a task to fall in love. But the song and dance numbers were great."

"Because the director was too ambitious," Chen Guiliang commented. "He wanted to cram everything in, and the musical numbers took up so much time that many things were only touched upon superficially and not explained clearly. It was neither profound nor simple, just hanging awkwardly in the middle. It's quite awkward. I reckon the director won't be trying this style again."

Bian Guanyue said, "I wonder if *The Promise* is any good."

At this very moment, Guo Feng and Shijie were still sitting in the movie theater.

"Hahahaha!"

A burst of laughter erupted, as if *The Promise* were a comedy.

Lines that were supposed to be touching always managed to make the entire audience burst into laughter. For example: "You've ruined my chance to be a good person."
